headline: Ran the warm filament to Wilmington, split time trolling and chunking — worth the fuel both ways
subhead: The canyon's still holding a strong yellowfin and white marlin bite heading into Labor Day, but the tropics are the only thing that can shut this down.
body_markdown:
The call this week for anyone burning fuel to Wilmington is simple: troll the early morning temp break, then switch to the chunk bucket once the fleet starts marking bait and the sun gets up. That's the pattern that's been paying off, and there's no reason to overthink it while the warm water's sitting where it is.

The Gulf Stream filament that's been feeding this canyon all summer hasn't broken down, and that's the whole story right now. We flagged this last week — said conditions looked set to hold through the near term with tropical development the only real threat — and that's exactly how it's played out. No storms have pushed through to mix things up, so the warm tongue is still draped over the grounds, still holding bait, and still holding fish. That's the kind of stability you don't get every September, so anyone with a weather window and the fuel budget should be using it.

For boats running out of Cape May or Indian River, the math still works if you're planning a full troll-and-chunk day rather than a quick strike. Burn the run out early, get lines in on the temper break along the canyon edge before the sun's fully up, and work the color changes where the clean blue meets the greener inshore water. That edge has been holding yellowfin and white marlin both, and the temperature line is doing exactly what it's supposed to do this time of year — stacking bait against the drop and giving the tuna and billfish a reason to sit right on it instead of running the open water.

Spread-wise, nothing fancy is required. A dredge with mullet or squid rigs up the middle, ballyhoo naked and rigged behind Sea Witches on the long riggers, and a couple of small cedar plugs or Green Machines in the shorts has been enough to draw both species into the pattern. White marlin have been eating the naked ballyhoo pulled just outside the wake, and once you raise one, it's worth dropping back a pitch bait — a ballyhoo on a circle hook — rather than trying to keep trolling through a school. Yellowfin have shown a preference for anything with some flash and speed in the mix, so a spreader bar with cut-eye Ilanders on the corners has been earning its spot in a lot of spreads this week.

Once the sun's up and the morning troll bite slows, that's the cue to switch over. Boats sliding into a chunk pattern along the canyon drop-off have been doing well on butterflied bunker and diced-up bluefish chunks fished on 50s and 30s, slow-trolling or drifting right on the temp line. Bigeye have been part of that mix after dark for the boats willing to stay out and work a chunk slick into the evening, with 6/0 circle hooks on fluorocarbon leader picking up the better-grade fish that won't come up for a bar rig in daylight.

Wahoo have been a bonus rather than a target — a couple of boats picked up fish on high-speed trolled lures worked around structure and current breaks on the run out, in that 12 to 18 knot range with a straight wire leader. Mahi have been scattered around any floating debris or grass lines holding along the edge, and it's worth having a couple of rods rigged with small ballyhoo or a bucktail ready to pitch if you spot a color change or a patch of weed — they'll show up when you're not necessarily fishing for them, and it's an easy add to the fish box if the crew's willing to slow down for a few minutes.

Honest read on effort versus result: this has not been an easy-money bite where every trolling pass turns a fish. It's been a grind-it-out pattern where the boats putting in the hours on the temp break and staying disciplined about switching to chunk when the troll goes quiet are the ones coming back with a mixed bag of yellowfin, a white marlin release or two, and the occasional wahoo or mahi. The days of just running out and getting bit on autopilot aren't here — you're working for it, but the work is paying off often enough to justify the fuel.

Looking ahead through Labor Day week, there's no reason to expect a dramatic shift. The warm water isn't going anywhere on its own, and the tuna and billfish activity should stay strong as long as nothing spins up in the tropics to mix the canyon. That's still the single biggest variable — any tropical system tracking up the Atlantic basin could churn this setup and cool the surface temps fast, so keep an eye on the extended tropical outlook before committing to a multi-day trip. Absent that, the smart play through the holiday weekend is the same one that's worked all week: early troll on the edge, chunk bucket ready for when the morning bite fades, and enough fuel in reserve to work the drop-off until the fish tell you otherwise.
